title: From Lab to Market: The US Push to Commercialise Quantum Technology
summary: The US launched a major 2026 effort to commercialise quantum technology, combining a US$2.013 billion Department of Commerce incentive, two executive orders on post-quantum cryptography and quantum innovation, and initiatives such as the Department of Energy's "Quantum Genesis" and DIU's "Farseer". The measures target supply chains, workforce, technology protection and commercialization to counter China and accelerate military and commercial applications.
content:
Author: Prateek Tripathi

The United States' biggest quantum push since 2018 combines funding, regulation and industrial policy to overcome quantum technology's biggest hurdle—commercialisation.

Following the announcement of a US$2 billion federal incentive for Quantum Technology (QT) by the US Department of Commerce (DoC) in May 2026, the Trump administration doubled down, signing two executive orders — one on Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) migration, and the other on the broader advancement of the US Quantum Information Science and Technology (QIST) ecosystem. This has been accompanied by the announcement of the "Quantum Genesis" initiative by the Department of Energy (DoE), as well as a multi-phase quantum sensing initiative by the Defence Innovation Unit (DIU). Taken together, these measures constitute Washington's most significant step towards QT advancement since the National Quantum Initiative Act (NQIA) in 2018 and clearly signal the US intent to establish itself as the global leader in the field.

Central to the package is a US$2.013 billion federal incentive announced by the DoC on 21 May 2026 under the CHIPS and Science Act. The DoC signed nine letters of intent: seven with quantum computing companies and two with domestic quantum foundry firms. To ensure accountability, the DoC will take a minority stake in each recipient company as a condition for disbursing funds. The incentives adopt a portfolio approach that simultaneously develops domestic capabilities across multiple quantum computing modalities while addressing critical hardware and engineering challenges. They align with other US efforts, such as DARPA's Quantum Benchmarking Initiative, which involves many of the same companies.

On 22 June 2026, President Donald Trump signed two executive orders. The first, titled "Securing the Nation Against Advanced Cryptographic Attacks", aims to mitigate risks posed by large-scale Cryptographically Relevant Quantum Computers (CRQCs) to existing encryption protocols. The order seeks to accelerate the transition to Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC) through coordination, acceleration, and procurement measures designed to replace vulnerable cryptographic systems across government and critical infrastructure.

The second order, titled "Ushering in the Next Frontier of Quantum Innovation", is a holistic effort to fortify US QT supply chains while accelerating commercialisation and deployment across quantum computing, communication (networking) and sensing. It includes technology protection measures, workforce expansion, and enhanced international engagement strategies intended to secure leadership across all key categories of QT.

Complementing the DoC funding and executive orders, the DoE announced the Quantum Genesis initiative on 23 June 2026. In line with Executive Order 14413, Quantum Genesis aims to develop a fault-tolerant quantum computer by 2028. At the same time, the DIU unveiled a multi-phase US$200 million program called "Farseer" to provide next-generation quantum sensing capabilities to the US Joint Force.

Taken together, these initiatives represent a targeted and comprehensive push by Washington to cement US leadership in QT in the near term. The strategy combines direct financing, partial equity stakes for oversight, regulatory and procurement levers, workforce development, and security-focused trade and technology protections. Many of these steps are explicitly designed to counter China's growing role in critical mineral supply chains and its emerging strengths in QT hardware supply chains.

The geopolitical dimension is explicit: several measures are aimed at preventing the US from being overtaken by a rapidly evolving Chinese QT ecosystem. Beyond competition for technological leadership, the dual-use nature of quantum technologies raises potential military implications, increasing the strategic importance of establishing secure domestic supply chains and rapid commercialisation pathways.

Despite strong R&D capabilities, the US has struggled to achieve commercial scalability in quantum hardware. The renewed push could be a game-changer by aligning federal funding, procurement, and policy to lower commercialization barriers and accelerate the transition from lab prototypes to market-ready systems.

Looking further ahead, the measures are likely to shape the broader trajectory of QT. Quantum technologies are expected to influence future technological development across fields such as digital simulation, sensing, navigation and secure communications. By mobilising funding, regulatory tools and industrial policy now, the US aims not only to capture economic value but also to shape standards, supply chains and norms around quantum applications.

Prateek Tripathi is an Associate Fellow at the Centre for Security, Strategy and Technology (CSST), Observer Research Foundation. His work focuses on emerging and deep technologies, including quantum.
